newsitem.title: UK: New Zealand bonds poised to gain after election.
newsitem.headline: New Zealand bonds poised to gain after election.

text.p: Bond investors willing to take a gamble ahead of general elections in New Zealand this weekend will be rewarded with hefty winnings as the political dust settles, analysts said on Wednesday.

Having spiralled lower in recent weeks as concerns over the poll's outcome grew, the country's debt market now offers good value against U.S. Treasuries and is set for a spate of fairly dramatic outperformance within the dollar-bloc, they said.
"Investors around the globe are still chasing yield," said Robin Marshall, chief economist at Chase in London.
"And New Zealand is one of the few relatively high-yield structures left. The money will pour in once the uncertainty is resolved."

Until recently, the ruling National Party was way ahead in opinion polls, but latest surveys show the main opposition Labour Party and its left-wing coalition partners nipping at the government's heels. With elections being decided by proportional representation for the first time in New Zealand, analysts said additional jitters in the market could be put down to a feeling that the likely outcome would be some sort of coalition leadership.

"The reason for the (recent) sell-off is the new election system," said Stephen Lewis, director of research at London Bond Broking Company. "The outcome is very uncertain -- but the most likely will be a coalition based around the Labour Party. Lewis said he thought this would give a boost to New Zealand's capital markets, since he expected a Labour-led administration to commit itself to tight fiscal policies.

Chase's Marshall said Australia, whose political uncertainties are basically resolved for the next three years, had seen its debt market benefit as investors ducked away from New Zealand and sought refuge there.

But he said those switches were likely to be reversed as New Zealand emerges from the election cloud and investors realise that even a change to a left-wing coalition would not necessarily mean looser government purse strings.

"There is a risk it will go a bit lower in the short-term if we get an indecisive result, but the market is getting to the stage where some form of coalition is more or less discounted so you could say we're near the bottom of this sell-off." "New Zealand's real yields are very attractive in the international context. This could well represent a buying opportunity in the medium term," Marshall said.
New Zealand's real yields, adjusted for inflation, are currently just under six percent at 10-years duration. Inflation in the year to June was at 2.33 percent.
Michael Derks, international fixed income strategist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, saw substantial worth in Kiwi bonds.
"New Zealand is oversold. Buying 10-year bonds at 150 basis points over U.S. Treasuries is very good value," he said.
"Once the political situation clarifies itself...the inherent value of this market will become apparent to overseas investors. They won't be shy in coming forward."
Derks said he though the 10-year spread to Treasuries would come in to 100 basis points in the next three to four months. LBB's Lewis said the move may be more dramatic.
"One of the features of the New Zealand market is that once it gets going it can move very fast," he said. "We might well see a 120 spread by the end of this month."
